q: `let a = 5; let b = a; b = 10;` What is `a` now?
options: `5`: `b` got its own copy of the number
why: A number is a simple value. `b = a` puts a copy of 5 in `b`'s own slot. Changing `b` does not touch `a`.

q: What does this print? Type the three answers with spaces between them.
why: `b = a` copies the arrow, so `a` and `b` are one object and `a.n` is `2`. `a === b` compares arrows, which are the same, so `true`. Two new `{ n: 2 }` are two objects with two arrows, so `false`.

q: Two objects with the same content are `===` to each other.
why: No. `===` on objects compares the arrows, not the content. Two `{ }` make two objects, so two different arrows. To compare content, compare the fields you care about, like `a.id === b.id`.

q: `const copy = { ...user }` is a shallow copy. Then you run `copy.address.city = "Bandung"`. What happens to `user.address.city`?
why: Spread copies one level. The `address` field holds an arrow, and the arrow is copied. Both objects point at one address object.

q: Which of these give a copy where changing `copy.address.city` does NOT change `user`?
why: `structuredClone` copies every level. The third one copies the `address` level on purpose. `{ ...user }` and `Object.assign` copy one level only, so `address` is still shared.

q: What does this print? Type the two answers with a space between them.
why: `push` changes the caller's array through the arrow, so `mine.length` is `1`. Then `list = [9]` points only the function's own slot at a new array. `mine` still points at the old one, and `out` is the new `[9]`, so `out[0]` is `9`.

q: `sortedNames(names)` returns `list.sort()`. After the call, what is true about the array `names`?
options: It is now sorted too, because `sort` changes the array in place
It is unchanged, because the function got a copy of the array
why: A parameter gets a copy of the arrow, not a copy of the array. `sort` changes the one shared array. Fix: `[...list].sort()`.

q: In React you run `cart.items.push("milk"); setCart(cart);`. The screen does not change. Why?
options: `cart` is still the same object, so React sees the same arrow and skips drawing
`push` does not work on arrays inside state
React draws again only after a second click
why: React compares the old and new arrow with `Object.is`. You changed the object in place and passed the same arrow, so React thinks nothing changed. Make a new object and a new array: `setCart({ ...cart, items: [...cart.items, "milk"] })`.

q: Put what JavaScript does in the right order.
items: Make the object with `name: "Ana"` and put an arrow to it in `user`
`const other = user` copies the arrow into `other`. No new object
`other.name = "Budi"` follows the arrow and changes the one object
`user.name` follows its arrow to the same object and gives `"Budi"`
why: Only one object exists the whole time. Two variables hold arrows to it.

code: const copy = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ when: new Date() }));
why: JSON has no date type. `JSON.stringify` turns the date into a text, and `JSON.parse` leaves it as text. So `copy.when.getFullYear()` is a `TypeError`.

q: Which of these change when you copy with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))`?
options: A field set to `undefined` is gone
why: JSON only keeps text, numbers, `true`, `false`, `null`, arrays and plain objects. A `Date` becomes text, an `undefined` field disappears, `NaN` becomes `null`, a `Map` or `Set` becomes `{}`, and a function is dropped.

q: What does this print? Type the answer.
why: `copy` is shallow, so `copy.address` is the same object as `user.address`. Setting the city to `"Bandung"` through `copy` changes `user` too. `deep` is a full copy, so changing it to `"Medan"` does not touch `user`.

q: `structuredClone` can copy an object that holds a function.
why: No. `structuredClone` keeps `Date`, `Map` and `Set`, but it throws an error (`DataCloneError`) if the data holds a function. The JSON way does not throw, but it silently drops the function.
